verdicts.note: The core risk is confirmed by xprem's own docs: the server signs every manifest with a key held in PostgreSQL, and signing is meant to stop a compromised bucket or CDN, not whoever can publish. The unrecoverable master key, the Enterprise-only IP allowlist and SSO, and the dashboard on the same server are confirmed. Because OTA JavaScript runs inside the binary that App Attest and Play Integrity vouch for, the publish path is part of the attendance trust boundary, so high severity stands. One claim and one recommended step are wrong or unsupported (see correction).
verdicts.correction: Wrong: 'Line 519's offline backup only works if the key is generated outside xprem first.' In the database key store the private key is sealed inside PostgreSQL, so an offline copy of the master key plus the normal backup of the xprem database preserves it. Line 519 should name the xprem master key and the xprem database instead of a key file. Unsupported: 'generate the key with eoas generate-certs and give it to xprem on first boot'. On a control-plane server the documented stores are 'database' (the server generates the pair) and 'aws-secrets-manager' (own pair, adds AWS). Local or environment keys reach the database only through the stateless or v2 migration, and stateless mode needs an Expo access token. The 'not on the internet' part is directly supported: BIND_TO_ADDRESS=127.0.0.1 behind the reverse proxy, and USE_DASHBOARD can stay off.

evidence.quote: xprem signs every update it serves. Your app embeds the matching certificate at build time and verifies that signature before applying an update so a compromised bucket or CDN can't push malicious code to your users.
It is the only thing that can decrypt your signing keys, and there is no recovery path. Recovering means generating new signing keys, rebuilding your app, and shipping it through the app stores.
File paths and environment variables are not offered here, because they cannot be provisioned per app for every replica.
If your keys were in `local` or `environment` mode, the same key pair is sealed into the database under the master key, so signed manifests keep verifying and no rebuild is needed.
Address the server listens on. Defaults to `0.0.0.0`, every interface. Set `127.0.0.1` to keep the server on the loopback interface behind a reverse proxy on the same host.
Token access rules, which scope an API key to the branches whose names match the patterns you give it, and restrict where it may be used from with an IP allowlist

recommendation_issues.problem: Two problems. (1) 'Generate the key myself and hand it to xprem on first boot' has no documented path on a fresh control-plane server. The documented routes either add AWS Secrets Manager (a new external dependency, fails compact) or start in stateless mode with an Expo token, which contradicts S12-F4's 'no Expo account'. The compact, documented option: keep the database key store, put the xprem master key on the offline backup list (line 519) and keep the xprem database inside the normal PostgreSQL backup. (2) 'Dashboard only through an SSH tunnel' and 'publish token only in CI' pull against each other. The publish routes live on the same server as the manifest, so a CI runner outside the server needs them public, and there the app-scoped token is the only guard (branch scoping and IP allowlists are Enterprise). The plan must pick one: publish from my own machine through the tunnel, or keep the publish routes public and guard the token like the signing key.

The bucket passes the compact lens, but for a different reason than given. xprem tolerates local storage on a single production instance. The real gain is pre-signed URLs: phones fetch bundles from the bucket, so assets that 'can be tens of megabytes' per device do not cross the shared API server at class start. The pin must also cover the eoas CLI, not only the image: a v3.2.0 or later server rejects publishes from an older eoas.

A hand-bumped runtimeVersion depends on memory, and forgetting it is exactly the failure the finding describes. A deterministic guard needs no new dependency: @expo/fingerprint already ships with expo 57.0.26. CI records the native fingerprint when it starts a native build and blocks an OTA publish when the fingerprint changed but runtimeVersion did not. Both values come from CI, which avoids the CI-versus-local mismatch xprem warns about.

Incomplete. The demo instructor also needs an exemption from the 3-device limit in line 69, because each review may run on a new device. Reviewers often try account deletion with the demo account, so the demo accounts must recreate themselves to stay 'non-expiring'. The fixed code must open only the demo course.

'Bireysel hesabımla başvururum' is stated as a given. It leaves out that my legal name becomes the public seller name and that guideline 5.2.1 may still push toward İÜ's account (see misses). Deciding before the first TestFlight build is right; the account choice should be written as an open decision with both sides.

'Otomatik yenilemeyi açarım' may not be available: Apple says website auto-renew exists only in certain regions. Fallback: enrol through the Apple Developer app, which Apple sells as an auto-renewable membership.

checked_ok_disputes.claim: xprem handles the plan's peak. Its manifest endpoint held p95 1.39 ms at 650 req/s on 1 vCPU, and bundle bytes are served by object storage, not by the server process.
checked_ok_disputes.problem: The numbers are right, but they only show that xprem copes when it runs alone. The benchmark ran xprem on its own 1 vCPU machine with a separate 2 vCPU PostgreSQL, wrote a device check-in for every poll (544 write IOPS at peak) and signed every response. The plan runs the API, worker, PostgreSQL and xprem in one Docker Compose (line 714), the research puts xprem's database on the same PostgreSQL server, and expo-updates polls on every cold start by default. At class start the polls, their database writes and the attendance sends therefore land on the same host and database together. Bytes skip the server only when a bucket is configured. The peak claim needs the polling change in misses (line 510).

misses.finding: The once-a-day rule covers only the plan's own version check. expo-updates runs its own check, by default on every cold start. Each poll reaches xprem, which signs the answer and, by default, writes a device check-in to its PostgreSQL database (at most one write per device per minute). xprem also sends an hourly usage ping by default. At the class-start peak (20,000 phones in 1 to 5 minutes) all of this lands on the same host and PostgreSQL server as the attendance sends. Phones that find a new update then start downloading assets that 'can be tens of megabytes' over campus Wi-Fi while the record is being sent. The research checked xprem's capacity but not the client's polling default.

verdict_reason: The only high-severity finding (S12-F5) holds in substance. One secondary claim and its key-import step are corrected from xprem's own docs, without weakening the risk. No finding is refuted or unverifiable, and every checked_ok item with a version, date, limit, fee or rule wording was confirmed. The one dispute (line 701 peak) is about co-location, not wrong numbers. New misses: three medium (expo-updates polling on every launch at class start, in-app account deletion for App Review, xprem's young control-plane mode and exit path) and three low. None is high, so the slice passes.
